reasoning: The underlying problem — that a small subset of EM eval questions suffices and that questions vary widely in their power to surface misalignment — is already substantially explored. The Model Organisms for EM paper (arXiv 2506.11613) already uses a curated 8-question "first plot" subset and states results on it "do not change conclusions" versus the full 48, and "The Devil in the Details" (arXiv 2511.20104) plus the LessWrong post "We need a better way to evaluate emergent misalignment" both document that question characteristics/format "substantially influence misalignment detection." However, no found work does the proposal's specific contribution: systematically rank every EM eval question by a per-item discriminative statistic (effect size / point-biserial / single-item AUC) between aligned and misaligned organisms, build minimal probe sets of size 1/3/5/10, and chart held-out cross-organism detection AUC vs probe-set size against the full suite. The Devil paper shows pooled question-level effects but no minimal-probe construction or size-vs-AUC tradeoff curve, and the LW post explicitly does not rank questions or propose reduced sets. The specific systematic minimal-probe optimization angle is unexplored, though it sits on a heavily-worked, low-counterfactual problem with public checkpoints readily available.

evidence.title: Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment
evidence.summary: Provides the open released EM model organisms and aligned counterparts the proposal would use, plus the standard eval question set and GPT-4o alignment/coherence judge. Already uses a curated 8-question 'first plot' subset and reports it does not change conclusions vs the full 48, establishing that a small subset suffices but without formalizing minimal-probe selection by discriminative power or cross-organism AUC.

evidence.title: The Devil in the Details: Emergent Misalignment, Format and Coherence in Open-Weights LLMs
evidence.summary: Across nine open-weights organisms, finds question characteristics (and format, e.g. JSON vs natural language) substantially influence whether misalignment is detected, and shows results across hand-picked question subsets. Demonstrates question-level variation in detection but does not rank individual questions by discriminative statistic, build minimal probe sets, or report detection AUC vs probe-set size against the full suite.

evidence.title: We need a better way to evaluate emergent misalignment
evidence.summary: Argues the 'one umbrella' EM eval conflates distinct behaviors and proposes refining the judge prompt to separate categories, using 48 pre-registered questions. Discusses evaluation methodology and shows hand-picked question subsets in an appendix but explicitly does not analyze individual-question diagnostic value, propose minimal question sets, or do AUC/detection-cost tradeoff analysis.

evidence.title: Point-biserial correlation for item discrimination
evidence.summary: Confirms point-biserial item discrimination is a standard, off-the-shelf statistic for ranking test items by how well they separate high vs low performers — the proposal applies this established psychometric tool to EM eval questions, indicating the proposed method itself is a well-known technique transplanted to a new (but heavily studied) detection setting.
